summary:
ELYSIUM IV is a browser-based interactive 3D Mars exploration and survival assessment experience developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Using real NASA Mars orbital data and a custom built 3D environment, it allows users to explore Elysium Planitia, operate an exploration rover, investigate terrain and soil samples, monitor environmental conditions, and record scientific observations.

The experience features three progressive missions: SOL 01, SOL 02, and SOL 03, guiding users through different stages of Martian exploration and environmental assessment.

ELYSIUM IV aims to make planetary exploration more accessible by transforming NASA data into an immersive experience that helps users understand Martian terrain and the challenges of future human exploration.

ELYSIUM IV is an independent educational simulation and is not an official NASA product. Simulated readings and analysis are not scientifically validated measurements.

1. Project Overview

ELYSIUM IV is a browser-based, interactive 3D Martian exploration and survival-assessment experience developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project combines real NASA Mars orbital data with a custom-built 3D simulation environment to allow users to explore selected regions of Mars, investigate surface characteristics, monitor environmental conditions, and document observations through a structured three-SOL mission journey.

The project focuses on Elysium Planitia, a region on Mars that is scientifically interesting for studying its surface features and considering potential locations for future human exploration. Rather than presenting Mars as a simple 3D landscape, ELYSIUM IV provides an interactive mission experience in which users can navigate across terrain, operate a custom-designed exploration rover, inspect essential resources, investigate soil samples, capture geological observations, and review mission records.

The experience is structured around three missions: SOL 01, SOL 02, and SOL 03. Each SOL introduces a different stage of the exploration and assessment process, progressively building a record of the user's observations and mission activities.

Our primary objective is to demonstrate how publicly available NASA planetary data can be transformed into an accessible and interactive 3D exploration experience. ELYSIUM IV aims to help users better understand Martian terrain, experience the challenges of surface exploration, and consider the environmental and operational factors that would matter when planning future human missions.

ELYSIUM IV is an independent educational and interactive simulation. It is not an official NASA product, and its simulated environmental readings and soil-analysis outputs should not be interpreted as scientifically validated measurements or conclusions about actual human habitability.

2. NASA Data and Scientific Foundation

A central part of ELYSIUM IV is the use of real Martian surface data obtained from NASA's High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE), an instrument aboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO).

We selected HiRISE Digital Terrain Model (DTM) products and their associated orthographic surface images. These datasets provide the scientific foundation for constructing the terrain used in the simulation.

We used two selected HiRISE DTM datasets covering locations in Elysium Planitia. The first dataset is used for the SOL 01 and SOL 02 exploration environment, while the second dataset is used for the SOL 03 environment.

How the NASA data is used

Digital Terrain Models (DTMs)

The DTM files contain elevation information representing the surface topography of Mars. These elevation values are used as the foundation for constructing the 3D terrain.

Instead of creating an entirely fictional landscape, we use the elevation information from the selected NASA datasets to establish the underlying terrain structure. This allows the simulation to represent surface variations such as slopes, depressions, elevated areas, and other topographic features.

Orthographic Surface Images

The associated HiRISE orthographic images provide visual information about the Martian surface. They are used as surface-image references and terrain texturing inputs for the 3D environment.

Combining elevation information with surface imagery allows us to build an environment that is based on actual orbital observations rather than a completely manually imagined landscape.

Data preparation and integration

The original NASA products are scientific data files rather than ready-to-use game-engine terrain assets. Therefore, they require preparation before they can be integrated into a real-time 3D environment.

Our development workflow includes inspecting and preparing the source terrain data, extracting the information needed for terrain construction, and integrating the resulting terrain representation into the Three.js environment.

We use geospatial data-processing tools, including GDAL-based workflows, as part of the terrain-data preparation process. The prepared terrain information is then used by our custom terrain implementation.

The final terrain is integrated into the browser-based experience with appropriate scale, visual representation, navigation, and rover interaction.

3. Selected Mars Locations and NASA Source Files

The following are the two principal HiRISE DTM datasets used as the foundation for the three-SOL environment.

Dataset 01 — SOL 01 and SOL 02

Location: Elysium Planitia, Mars

Approximate project reference coordinates:

  • Latitude: 6.5919° N
  • Longitude: 155.2032° E

NASA HiRISE DTM file:

DTEEC_017983_1865_017838_1865_A01.IMG

Associated orthographic image used in the project:

ESP_017983_1865_RED_A_01_ORTHO.JP2

Official HiRISE dataset page:

https://hirise.lpl.arizona.edu/dtm/ESP_017983_1865

This dataset provides the elevation and surface-image foundation for the SOL 01 and SOL 02 environment. The same selected terrain region is used across these two missions, allowing the user to continue the exploration experience through different mission stages and environmental conditions.

Dataset 02 — SOL 03

Location: Elysium Planitia, Mars

Approximate dataset centre coordinates:

  • Latitude: 0.87° N
  • Longitude: 160.6° E

NASA HiRISE DTM file:

DTEEC_004151_1810_020963_1810_U01.IMG

Associated orthographic image used in the project:

PSP_004151_1810_RED_A_01_ORTHO.JP2

Official HiRISE dataset page:

https://hirise.lpl.arizona.edu/dtm/PSP_004151_1810

This dataset represents a separate area in Elysium Planitia and provides the terrain foundation for SOL 03. It allows the final mission to introduce a different Martian landscape for geological and environmental observation.

Understanding the two data products

The DTM and orthographic image serve different purposes:

  • The .IMG DTM product provides the elevation information used to construct terrain geometry.
  • The .JP2 orthographic image provides the corresponding surface imagery used for visual representation and texturing.

The coordinates above identify the approximate project reference or dataset centre. They should not be interpreted as the exact coordinates of every point across the playable terrain.

Data attribution: NASA / Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) / University of Arizona — HiRISE, with the SOL 03 DTM product identified as a USGS-produced product in its file identifier.

4. Custom 3D Development and Asset Creation

One of the main development principles behind ELYSIUM IV is that the core 3D exploration environment was built by our team rather than assembled from a collection of ready-made Mars simulation assets.

We designed and developed the major project-specific 3D components ourselves, including the terrain environments, exploration vehicle, vehicle interior, and supporting interactive environments.

Blender was used for 3D modelling and asset preparation, while Three.js was used to integrate and render the interactive 3D experience in the browser.

4.1 Custom Martian Terrain Development

The terrain is one of the most important technical components of ELYSIUM IV.

Our terrain environments are based on the selected NASA HiRISE DTM datasets. We use the elevation data as the foundation for generating the terrain surface, rather than relying on manually sculpted landscapes as the sole source of topography.

The terrain data is prepared for integration into the 3D environment, where the elevation information is represented through custom terrain geometry. The corresponding surface imagery supports the visual appearance of the landscape.

The resulting terrain environments are integrated into Three.js and configured for real-time exploration.

We also developed the terrain environments with the practical requirements of interactive navigation in mind. The user must be able to travel across the terrain, operate the rover, reach designated mission checkpoints, and interact with the mission environment.

Each selected terrain region is integrated into its corresponding SOL configuration.

4.2 Custom Exploration Rover

The exploration vehicle used in ELYSIUM IV is a custom-built 3D asset created for the project.

The rover was modelled and prepared using Blender, rather than relying on a ready-made rover asset as the main project vehicle.

The custom vehicle is designed to function as the primary transportation system during the Martian exploration missions.

Its implementation includes:

  • A custom 3D rover model.
  • A dedicated vehicle interior.
  • A driving and steering interaction system.
  • Vehicle entry and exit interactions.
  • Wheel and vehicle movement behaviour.
  • Interior and exterior lighting.
  • Interactive cockpit displays and control screens.
  • Mission-related vehicle information and resource displays.

The rover is integrated into the Three.js environment and connected to the terrain navigation and mission progression systems.

4.3 Custom Rover Interior and Interactive Cockpit

The rover interior is another project-specific 3D environment designed and modelled using Blender.

Instead of presenting the rover as a simple external vehicle model, we created an interior space that users can enter and interact with.

The interior includes a cockpit layout, walkable areas, interactive screens, lighting elements, and designated control sections.

The interactive displays represent different operational and environmental information, including:

  • Oxygen status.
  • Water and nutrition resources.
  • Battery status.
  • Cabin pressure.
  • Carbon dioxide information.
  • Environmental conditions.
  • Temperature.
  • General vehicle status.
  • Driving and navigation-related information.

The screens and interaction points are connected to the project's custom interaction systems. This allows the user to inspect relevant information while operating or preparing to operate the rover.

The interior was designed as part of the overall exploration experience, making the vehicle an interactive mission environment rather than simply a means of transportation.

4.4 Custom Mission Environments and Interactive Systems

The project also includes custom-designed mission environments, checkpoints, navigation points, and interactive locations.

These components are integrated into the Three.js experience and connected to the mission-management system.

The implementation includes:

  • SOL-specific terrain environments.
  • Mission starting locations.
  • Rover spawning and placement points.
  • Checkpoints.
  • Mission finishing locations.
  • Environmental inspection interactions.
  • Soil investigation interactions.
  • Observation and photography interactions.
  • Mission information interfaces.
  • Mission progression and completion validation.

The mission environments are configured to support the intended progression of each SOL without introducing unrelated mission stages.

5. Three-SOL Mission Implementation

ELYSIUM IV is structured around exactly three Martian exploration missions. Each SOL represents a different stage of the exploration process.

The missions are connected through a progression system. Completing the required objectives in one SOL allows the user to continue to the next stage.

SOL 01 — Initial Martian Exploration

Mission objective: Explore the first selected Martian terrain, become familiar with the rover and its operational systems, inspect essential resources, and record initial environmental observations.

SOL 01 introduces the user to the exploration environment and the main interaction systems.

The mission begins at a designated starting location. The user approaches the custom-built rover and enters it using the interaction system.

Once inside, the user can access the rover's cockpit and inspect the available mission information and operational displays.

The initial mission activities include:

  1. Starting the exploration mission.
  2. Reviewing the initial mission information and telemetry.
  3. Inspecting the available water and nutrition resources.
  4. Checking environmental information and available tools.
  5. Entering and operating the exploration rover.
  6. Navigating across the NASA-data-based Martian terrain.
  7. Reaching the designated checkpoint.
  8. Recording the required checkpoint observations.
  9. Continuing to the designated finishing location.

During the exploration, the mission system tracks the required activities and updates the relevant mission records.

At the end of SOL 01, the system validates the required objectives, saves the mission information, and unlocks SOL 02.

Purpose of SOL 01: Introduce the user to Martian surface exploration, rover operation, resource inspection, and basic environmental observation.

SOL 02 — Daytime Soil Investigation

Mission objective: Conduct a simulated surface-soil investigation under daytime Martian environmental conditions and document the observations.

SOL 02 continues from the completion point of SOL 01.

The user transitions to the next mission through the mission interaction system. Before the new environment is loaded, the system validates the previous mission's completion and saves the relevant mission records.

SOL 02 introduces a daytime environment, creating a different visual and operational setting for the exploration.

The mission begins near the designated rover location. The user can review the previous mission records and inspect available resources and environmental information.

The main mission activities include:

  1. Reviewing the previous SOL records.
  2. Inspecting water and nutrition resources.
  3. Checking environmental information and available tools.
  4. Navigating towards the designated soil-investigation area.
  5. Using the navigation beam and mission guidance to locate the checkpoint.
  6. Exiting the rover and entering the EVA exploration state.
  7. Monitoring the oxygen HUD while outside the rover.
  8. Reaching the soil-investigation interaction point.
  9. Activating the soil-investigation interaction.
  10. Recording observations about the sample, including its visible colour, texture, observed moisture, and additional notes.
  11. Returning to the rover with the recorded sample information.
  12. Transferring the sample to the designated storage or rack area.
  13. Confirming the sample transfer.
  14. Reviewing the available illustrative analysis and generating the mission report.
  15. Travelling to the SOL 02 finishing location.

The soil-investigation stage is designed to demonstrate a structured observation workflow. The user records visible and simulated sample characteristics, and the mission system uses these observations to support the in-game investigation report.

Any displayed sample-analysis information is illustrative or simulated. It is not a laboratory result, a direct NASA soil measurement, or a scientifically verified determination of the sample's composition.

At the end of the mission, the system validates the required objectives and saves the relevant mission logs, sample observations, analysis information, and report. Successful completion unlocks SOL 03.

Purpose of SOL 02: Demonstrate how an interactive exploration system can guide users through a structured surface investigation, sample documentation, and mission reporting process.

SOL 03 — Geological and Environmental Assessment

Mission objective: Explore a separate selected Martian terrain region, capture geological observations, document environmental information, and produce a combined mission record.

SOL 03 is the final stage of the ELYSIUM IV exploration journey.

After completing SOL 02, the user transitions to the SOL 03 environment. The system validates the previous mission, saves the required records, and loads the separate terrain environment based on the second selected NASA HiRISE dataset.

The mission introduces a new exploration area with daytime environmental conditions.

The main activities include:

  1. Reviewing the records from SOL 01 and SOL 02.
  2. Inspecting the available resources and environmental information.
  3. Checking the tools and mission equipment.
  4. Entering the existing exploration rover.
  5. Navigating towards the designated SOL 03 checkpoint.
  6. Exiting the rover and activating the observation camera.
  7. Capturing images of visible Martian geological and terrain features.
  8. Saving the required observation photographs.
  9. Returning to the rover.
  10. Reviewing the captured images through the Mission OS.
  11. Writing and saving the geological research log.
  12. Documenting observations about terrain features, mountains, directions, temperature information, and additional notes.
  13. Travelling to the final SOL 03 finishing location.
  14. Reviewing the combined mission history from all three SOLs.
  15. Completing the final report and resource confirmations.

The observation camera allows the user to capture views from the simulation and preserve them as part of the mission record. The captured photographs are used as visual documentation for the final assessment.

The research log allows the user to record observations and connect them with the exploration activities completed during the previous missions.

Once the required tasks, observations, report, and confirmations are complete, the user can activate the final Complete Journey action.

The system then records the final mission completion and presents the project's existing final video sequence.

Purpose of SOL 03: Bring together the exploration, soil-investigation, geological-observation, and environmental-recording activities into a final mission assessment.

6. Mission OS and Data Persistence

ELYSIUM IV includes a custom Mission OS interface that acts as the user's main information and mission-management system.

It provides access to mission instructions, task progression, environmental information, resource status, investigation records, photographs, and reports.

The Mission OS is connected to the mission-management implementation so that the user can review relevant information throughout the three-SOL journey.

The system is designed to maintain mission progression and relevant records using browser-compatible persistence mechanisms.

This includes information such as:

  • Completed mission objectives.
  • SOL progression status.
  • Environmental inspection records.
  • Soil-investigation observations.
  • Sample-related information.
  • Captured observation photographs.
  • Research logs.
  • Mission reports.
  • Final journey completion status.

This persistence allows the user to continue through the structured mission experience while retaining the records generated during the exploration.

7. Technology and Development Tools

The project combines 3D modelling, geospatial data preparation, and browser-based real-time rendering.

Three.js

  • Real-time 3D rendering.
  • Martian terrain presentation.
  • Rover integration and interaction.
  • First-person exploration.
  • Environmental and mission interactions.
  • Scene management and visual presentation.

Blender

  • Custom rover modelling.
  • Custom rover interior modelling.
  • Project-specific 3D environment and asset creation.
  • Model preparation for integration into the browser-based 3D experience.

GDAL-based geospatial workflow

  • Inspection and preparation of the selected NASA terrain datasets.
  • Geospatial data handling as part of the terrain integration process.

NASA HiRISE Data

  • Digital Terrain Models for elevation-based terrain construction.
  • Orthographic images for Martian surface visual reference and texturing.

Browser Technologies

  • Browser-based application delivery.
  • Interactive user interfaces.
  • Mission progression.
  • Browser-compatible storage for mission records.

The project is designed to run as an accessible browser-based experience without requiring users to install a dedicated desktop simulation application.

8. What Makes ELYSIUM IV Different?

ELYSIUM IV combines real planetary observation data with custom-built interactive 3D development.

Its key contributions include:

1. NASA-data-based terrain environments

The terrain foundation comes from selected NASA HiRISE DTM products and associated orthographic imagery, rather than relying entirely on fictional or manually sculpted Martian landscapes.

2. Custom-built 3D assets

The project's main terrain environments, rover, rover interior, and supporting interactive elements were developed specifically for ELYSIUM IV using our own modelling and development workflow.

3. A connected three-SOL exploration journey

Instead of offering only a free-roaming Mars environment, the project provides a structured progression from initial exploration to soil investigation and final geological and environmental assessment.

4. Interactive rover operation

Users can enter and exit the rover, operate it, navigate the terrain, inspect cockpit information, and use it as the central transportation system throughout the missions.

5. Structured observation and documentation

The project allows users to record soil observations, capture geological photographs, write research logs, and review mission reports.

6. Accessible browser-based experience

The project brings together the 3D environment, mission interactions, and exploration systems in a browser-based application.

9. Project Goals and Potential Impact

ELYSIUM IV aims to make selected Martian surface data more accessible through interactive exploration.

The project demonstrates how scientific terrain products can be integrated into a real-time 3D environment to help users understand the relationship between surface topography, exploration routes, rover operation, and field observations.

Through its three-SOL structure, the experience introduces users to several considerations relevant to planning future human exploration:

  • Understanding the surrounding terrain.
  • Navigating across a planetary surface.
  • Monitoring essential resources.
  • Considering environmental conditions.
  • Conducting and documenting surface investigations.
  • Recording geological observations.
  • Reviewing mission information before making an overall assessment.

The project is intended as an educational and exploratory experience that can encourage interest in planetary science, space exploration, geospatial data, and interactive scientific visualisation.

It does not claim to determine whether a location is actually suitable for human settlement. Instead, it demonstrates how available orbital data and simulated exploration workflows can help users engage with the kinds of information that may be relevant to future mission planning.

11. Final Statement

ELYSIUM IV represents our effort to combine NASA planetary data, custom 3D modelling, and interactive browser-based development into a single Martian exploration experience.

By using real HiRISE terrain products as the foundation for our environments and developing our own rover, interior, terrain integration, and mission systems, we have created a three-stage exploration journey that allows users to experience Martian surface navigation, resource inspection, soil investigation, geological observation, and mission documentation.

Our goal is to transform complex planetary surface data into an engaging and accessible experience that encourages users to explore Mars, understand its terrain, and think about the challenges involved in future human exploration.
